The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Establish the building or structural-module category from massing, roof or overhead profile, entrance or connection hierarchy, structural bays, openings, and ground or support relationship before signage and color are visible. Keep the working envelope near 18 meters wide, 14 meters deep, and 9 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starline Clinic Exterior; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Model a coherent foundation, frame or load-bearing wall system, layered facade or structural depth, human-scale access, glazing or openings with frames, weather and drainage treatment, service access, and credible transitions between materials. Required visible components are primary massing, roof line, entrance, window system, facade material breaks, service side, foundation. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Place it on the parcel, terrain shelf, dock edge, modular foundation, or interior footprint named by the blueprint. Public access faces navigation and social space; service access faces the alley, utility corridor, backstage zone, waterfront service edge, or maintenance route. Foundation, stairs, ramps, porches, piles, retaining walls, and terrain transitions must meet the environment without floating gaps. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Keep entrances, shutters, gates, windows, awnings, stairs, ramps, elevators, signs, lighting, roof equipment, and service components separable whenever gameplay or state changes may need them. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use modular floor, wall, roof, stair, rail, counter, doorway, foundation, and major structural collision. Walkable areas, entrances, windows used for gameplay, and service openings must match the visible model, while trim, roof equipment, cables, fasteners, and inaccessible facade detail remain simplified or nonblocking. Use positive Z as the principal entrance, public face, or module-forward direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at ground level or the documented connection plane near the footprint center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve massing, entrances, openings, supports, and skyline in every LOD. Repeating windows, panels, rails, trim, and structural members should use shared geometry or instancing. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 39,000 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 18,000 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 6,000 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Establish the building or structural-module category from massing, roof or overhead profile, entrance or connection hierarchy, structural bays, openings, and ground or support relationship before signage and color are visible.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starline Clinic Exterior is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

productionBrief.placement: Place it on a named floor, wall, counter, workstation, classroom, bedroom, shop, restaurant, sanitary, storage, or service socket. Feet, wall brackets, plumbing, cable routes, backs, and user clearance must align with the room and nearby interaction positions.
productionBrief.silhouetteAndProportion: Seat or work height, depth, back angle, leg clearance, storage volume, support placement, and reachable controls must immediately explain how a person uses the object.
productionBrief.structuralConstruction: Model load-bearing frames, legs, pedestals, brackets, seams, cushions, panels, drawers, hinges, plumbing, glides, cable routing, fasteners, wall anchors, or floor anchors appropriate to the item.
requiredComponents: legs, pedestal, wall mount, or floor support

materialPlan.metalRule: Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material.
materialPlan.glassRule: Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane.
materialPlan.masonryRule: Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling.
materialPlan.woodRule: Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use.
materialPlan.flexibleRule: Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling.
materialPlan.emissiveRule: Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure.

townArtDirection.style: glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors

productionBrief.conditionAndWear: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection.

interactionAndAnimation.guidance: Preserve seats, drawers, doors, screens, lamps, cushions, controls, storage, plumbing fixtures, and movable surfaces as distinct objects when gameplay can sit, open, use, move, customize, or damage them.
hooks: seating, occupancy, or interaction sockets

productionBrief.collision: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision.
productionBrief.orientationAndPivot: Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center.
productionBrief.optimization: Keep ergonomic silhouette and contact points at every LOD. Repeated slats, legs, buttons, cushions, shelves, and fasteners should share meshes or instances.

Model it as a modular traversal, road, sidewalk, bridge, dock, platform, path, rail, or course asset designed to connect cleanly and support movement without floating or snagging geometry. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles. Keep the working envelope near 1.4 meters wide, 0.9 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Music Stage Platform; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Provide surface thickness, engineered edges, joints, drainage, markings, supports, retaining structure, barriers, and transition pieces. Elevated or marine modules require believable beams, columns, cables, piles, brackets, or anchors. Required visible components are primary instrument, microphone, light, camera-support, or backdrop assembly, load-bearing stand or frame, controls, keys, pads, clamps, or adjustment joints, cable, signal, or power routing, protective housing or case, operator or performer interaction position, floor feet, anchors, or counterweights. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Snap it to the road, path, bridge, dock, rail, platform, course, or terrain grid with exact edge continuity, matching elevation, consistent width, correct travel direction, believable support spacing, and continuous simplified collision. No gaps, overlaps, floating ends, or invisible ledges are allowed. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Define walk, drive, climb, jump, grind, checkpoint, hazard, fall, docking, and connection boundaries through named surfaces and sockets. Expected hooks include changeable display, content, or emissive state, day, night, powered, warning, and damaged light states. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use continuous simplified traversal collision matching grades, gaps, curbs, rails, docking edges, fall boundaries, and platform surfaces. Decorative cracks, bolts, grates, trim, and surface noise must not create snagging micro-collision. Use positive Z as the travel or module-continuation direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the documented grid center, connection edge, spline point, or docking plane. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use modular dimensions, shared materials, and continuous simplified collision. Distant LODs may reduce cracks and hardware but cannot change grade, gaps, width, edge safety, or traversal timing. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 14,040 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 6,480 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 2,160 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Music Stage Platform is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Roads and street props.” A production-ready Starline Planter, designed as a city planter for Starline City. The container needs wall thickness, rim depth, soil, drainage logic, and believable planting rather than a cube with a green sphere. The object must remain immediately recognizable from silhouette and required components, use physically coherent construction and human or vehicle scale, and follow the town direction: glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. This asset appears under the blueprint section “C. Roads and street props” and should visibly support that gameplay or environmental role rather than acting as generic filler. The blueprint evidence is: B. Modular architecture C. Roads and street props

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is vegetation because dedicated family planter resolves the physical object as vegetation. Model it as a botanically or ecologically coherent plant, tree, crop, coral, fungus, or landscaped growth asset with believable anchoring and growth hierarchy. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Species category and maturity must read from trunk, stem, branch rhythm, crown, leaf massing, roots, fronds, petals, coral arms, fungal caps, or planting container. Keep the working envelope near 1 meters wide, 1 meters deep, and 0.75 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starline Planter; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Build a clear hierarchy from roots or anchor through trunk, branches, stems, leaves, flowers, fruit, coral polyps, or other species structures rather than spheres or disconnected cards. Required visible components are outer planter body, inner soil volume, rim, drainage detail, planting. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Anchor it in soil, rock, a planter, cultivated bed, roof garden, seabed, coral substrate, wall pocket, or shoreline appropriate to the species. Root or attachment structure, growth direction, density, wind or current response, and navigation clearance must fit the environment. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Provide wind groups, harvest points, breakable regions, climbable trunks, collision roots, seasonal variants, and placement sockets where gameplay requires them. Expected hooks include wind, current, harvest, damage, growth, season, or placement-variation groups. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use trunk, major branch, root, planter, coral-anchor, or harvest collision only where gameplay needs blocking, climbing, damage, or collection. Leaves, petals, grass blades, and small fronds remain nonblocking. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use clusters, cards, instances, and impostors strategically while preserving species silhouette and branching logic and controlling overdraw. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 12,480 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 5,760 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 1,920 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Species category and maturity must read from trunk, stem, branch rhythm, crown, leaf massing, roots, fronds, petals, coral arms, fungal caps, or planting container.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starline Planter is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

assets.deepDescription:
Starline Streetlight Gold is the definitive production specification for prop_starline_streetlight_gold_a_v01.glb in starline-city. It originates from docs/STARLINE_CITY_BLUEPRINT.md under “C. Roads and street props.” A production-ready Starline Streetlight Gold, designed as a municipal streetlight for Starline City. Include weatherproof mounting, service access, a credible support arm, proper luminaire housing, and enough segment resolution for round metal parts. The object must remain immediately recognizable from silhouette and required components, use physically coherent construction and human or vehicle scale, and follow the town direction: glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. This asset appears under the blueprint section “C. Roads and street props” and should visibly support that gameplay or environmental role rather than acting as generic filler. The blueprint evidence is: B. Modular architecture C. Roads and street props

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is infrastructure because dedicated family streetlight resolves the physical object as infrastructure. Model it as a serviceable civic, industrial, marine, utility, transit, security, or public-realm asset whose installation, operation, protection, and maintenance logic are visible. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Recognition must come from the relationship between support, enclosure, operating surface, access point, protected hardware, and ground, wall, dock, road, or network connection. Keep the working envelope near 2.2 meters wide, 0.6 meters deep, and 6.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starline Streetlight Gold; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Include mounting, foundations or brackets, structural members, weather or pressure protection, access, hinges, latches, vents, conduit or cable paths, drainage, warnings, controls, and maintenance hardware as appropriate. Required visible components are base flange, anchor bolts, pole, maintenance access, support arm, luminaire housing, lens. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Install it on the named ground, curb, wall, road, dock, roof, utility corridor, platform, shoreline, or service foundation. Show anchors, brackets, conduits, piles, seals, drainage, clearance, and maintenance access so the device belongs to a real network rather than floating as decoration. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Separate controls, doors, lenses, lights, handles, hoses, nozzles, movable arms, covers, gates, scanners, cameras, and service components so systems can animate or change state. Expected hooks include day, night, powered, warning, and damaged light states. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve functional outline, installation, and operating surfaces. Repeated bolts, louvers, bars, lenses, posts, and rails should use instancing, while collision follows major volumes. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 10,920 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 5,040 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 1,680 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Recognition must come from the relationship between support, enclosure, operating surface, access point, protected hardware, and ground, wall, dock, road, or network connection.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starline Streetlight Gold is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is road_surface because strong filename prefix resolves the physical object as road_surface. Model it as a modular traversal, road, sidewalk, bridge, dock, platform, path, rail, or course asset designed to connect cleanly and support movement without floating or snagging geometry. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles. Keep the working envelope near 10 meters wide, 10 meters deep, and 0.3 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Starline Premiere; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Provide surface thickness, engineered edges, joints, drainage, markings, supports, retaining structure, barriers, and transition pieces. Elevated or marine modules require believable beams, columns, cables, piles, brackets, or anchors. Required visible components are surface slab, curbs or edges, lane or path markings, connection seams, drainage detail. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary painted architectural metal, glass, marquee lighting, backstage industrial hardware, warm marquee gold, black, deep red, violet, sunset orange, concrete gray. glamorous production city with real backstage labor; theaters, studios, hotels, hills, apartments, warehouses, lighting rigs, and service corridors. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: red-carpet-only city, empty studio facades, generic neon metropolis. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Snap it to the road, path, bridge, dock, rail, platform, course, or terrain grid with exact edge continuity, matching elevation, consistent width, correct travel direction, believable support spacing, and continuous simplified collision. No gaps, overlaps, floating ends, or invisible ledges are allowed. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Define walk, drive, climb, jump, grind, checkpoint, hazard, fall, docking, and connection boundaries through named surfaces and sockets. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use continuous simplified traversal collision matching grades, gaps, curbs, rails, docking edges, fall boundaries, and platform surfaces. Decorative cracks, bolts, grates, trim, and surface noise must not create snagging micro-collision. Use positive Z as the travel or module-continuation direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the documented grid center, connection edge, spline point, or docking plane. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use modular dimensions, shared materials, and continuous simplified collision. Distant LODs may reduce cracks and hardware but cannot change grade, gaps, width, edge safety, or traversal timing. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 7,800 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 3,600 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 1,200 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Edge profile, grade, lane or path width, curb or barrier, structural support, connection points, and travel direction must explain how the surface carries players or vehicles.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Starline Premiere is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.
